y-m-79-04.thinking.2: Revise Your Idea with New Information
y-m-79-04.title: They say shaved ice shop sales grew 30% in one month
y-m-79-04.topic: Seasonality in time-series data and year-over-year comparison
y-m-79-04.goal: Know why one-month growth rate alone makes growth hard to judge; refine using same month last year and added info (seat count).
y-m-79-04.material: Shaved-ice shop sales were 120만 원 in June and 156만 원 in July. Owner says, "Sales rise 30% in one month, our shop clearly growing fast!" (Unit 만 원. Assume same business-day count.)
y-m-79-04.thinking.1: Choose comparison base (previous month or same month last year) and calculate yourself
y-m-79-04.prereq.0: Task H3 (hard) assumes high-school elective 'Practical Statistics', not Ministry grade assignment. Prereqs: calculate growth percentage and read table. Seasonal variation explained as roughly yearly repeating seasonal effect.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.prompt: Are June 120만 원 and July 156만 원 enough to say shop grew?
y-m-79-04.s.s1.hint.0: Think when shaved-ice sales rise/fall and whether June-July change may repeat each year.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write which two numbers compare to confirm growth after removing seasonal effect.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.o.a: Enough. 30% monthly increase clearly huge growth.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.r.a: You read one-month jump as growth. For seasonal business like shaved ice, increase may repeat every year.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.o.b: Not enough. Need August sales to judge.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.r.b: No need wait August; change comparison base using existing data.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.o.c: Not enough. Need last year's sales for same months.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.r.c: This compares same months to filter seasonal effect.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.o.d: Not enough. Need sales distribution at other shops this year too.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.r.d: Comparing nearby shops useful, but no direct help to separate this shop's own seasonal rise.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.explain: June to July rise may be summer peak season. To separate growth from seasonal effect, need same-time data, like last year's June and July.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.acc.0: Other shops comparison also useful, but last-year same-month data more directly separates this shop seasonality.
y-m-79-04.s.s2.prompt: Last-year data arrived: sales were 100만 원 in June and 140만 원 in July. Explain how compare/calculate growth and what tell owner.
y-m-79-04.s.s2.hint.0: Pair this-year and last-year June and July values in table.
y-m-79-04.s.s2.hint.1: Find same-month increases and compare side by side with June-to-July growth rate.
y-m-79-04.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Compared with same month last year...
y-m-79-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: You compare same months (June with June, July with July)?
y-m-79-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You mention June-to-July growth similar last year too?
y-m-79-04.s.s2.model.0: Compare same months. June rose 100만 원 to 120만 원, +20%; July rose 140만 원 to 156만 원, about +11%. This year higher than last year, but growth rate slowed; June-to-July rise was 40% last year too, so summer effect large. 30%.
y-m-79-04.s.s2.model.1: Previous-month comparison mixes seasonality, so compare last year's June-July rise (40%) with this year's 30%. This year's growth slower. Sales exceed last year same months, so shop grew, but pace slowed.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.prompt: New info: shop increased seat count 20% versus last year at end of May. Including this, best interpretation of 'sales per seat' versus last year? (sales per seat = sales÷seats)
y-m-79-04.s.s3.hint.0: Divide this year's June and July sales each by 1.2 to convert to last year's seat count.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.hint.1: Put converted values beside same-month sales last year; compare equal, greater or smaller.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.o.a: June sales per seat same as last year; July fell about 7%.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.r.a: You consider seat growth too. June 120÷1.2=100, same as last year; July 156÷1.2=130, below last year's 140.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.o.b: Sales per seat rose from last year in both June and July.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.r.b: June sales grew 20%, seats grew 20% too. Matching growth rates makes sales per seat growth hard to claim.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.o.c: Seat count no effect on sales, so earlier reading remains.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.r.c: More seats mean more customers served at same time. Hard to say seats unrelated to sales.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.o.d: July sales per seat rose about 11%, more than June.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.r.d: You mistake 11% sales growth for sales-per-seat growth. Adjust for seats' 20% rise.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.explain: Seat count became 1.2 times as many. Divide this year's sales by 1.2: June 120÷1.2=100 (same as last year's 100); July 156÷1.2=130 (about 7.1% below last year's 140). Sales rose, but sales per seat stayed same or fell. If added seats caused sales growth, 'growth' means something different.

y-m-79-03.thinking.1: Finding several cases wey meet di conditions
y-m-79-03.title: A product called defective by '95% accurate' machine
y-m-79-03.topic: Conditional probability and test accuracy (base rate)
y-m-79-03.goal: Use counts to show among positive tests, truly defective share varies greatly with defect/base and misclassification rates; find multiple cases meeting conditions.
y-m-79-03.material:
Factory automatic inspection machine info:
- Defective items are 1% of all products.
- 95% of defective items are judged defective.
- 5% of normal items are wrongly judged defective.

Ad says '95% accuracy'. Student says, 'A product called defective is 95% likely truly defective,' and calculates using 10,000 items. 10000
y-m-79-03.thinking.2: Saying what ad phrase leaves out
y-m-79-03.prereq.0: Task H3 hard level for Practical Statistics elective, not grade assignment. Prerequisites: percentages/ratios and setting total to 10,000 to count. No probability formulas needed; if learned conditional probability, may verify same value. 10000
y-m-79-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose first wrong line in student's calculation.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.hint.0: Recalculate each line and check arithmetic.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.hint.1: In final ratio, compare 'what out of what' and whether denominator group matches 'products called defective' in question.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.line.0: If dem inspect 10,000 products, 100 defective and 9,900 normal. 10000; 9900.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.line.4: Of dem, really defective na 95, so true-defect share among defect judgments 95÷100=95%.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.explain: Lines 1–4 correct. Line 5 numerator 95 right, but divide by 590 ('all items judged defective'). 100 na truly defective item count, no answer question. 95÷590≈0.161, around 16.1%.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.prompt: Inspection machine defect rate p%, and wrongly call normal defective rate q%. (Still call 95% of defectives defective.) Assume many products; make 3 different (p,q) where at least half (50%) items flagged defective are truly defective. p,q integers 1 to 10.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.hint.0: Choose p,q and find among 10,000 products count truly defective and flagged defective, plus normal but flagged defective. 10000.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare those two counts; decide which must be bigger for at least half, change p or q one at a time.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.fail.c1: p and q must be between 1 and 10.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Enter p and q as integers.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.ok.c3: At least 50% of items flagged defective are truly defective.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.fail.c3: Among flagged products, truly defective less than half. Take 10,000 products and compare true-defect flags with normal items wrongly flagged. 10000.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.explain: With 10,000 products, true-defect flags =95×p and false flags among normal =q×(100−p). If first at least second, half or more flagged items truly defective. (2,1):190 vs 98; (5,5):475 vs 475 (exactly half); (10,3):950 vs 270. (1,1):95 vs 99, below half. 10000: 95×p; q×(100−p); (2,1)=190 vs 98; (5,5)=475; (10,3)=950; (1,1)=95 vs 99. More values: 1,1 gives 95 vs 99; 2,1 gives 190 vs 98; 5,5 gives 475; 10,3 gives 950. 10,000 products; 95 × p; q × (100 − p); (2, 1) 190 vs 98; (5, 5) 475 vs 475; (10, 3) 950 vs 270; (1, 1) 95 vs 99.
y-m-79-03.s.s3.prompt: For buyer seeing ad 'Accuracy 95%' and thinking 'if flagged defective, 95% truly defective', explain what this number alone cannot tell and what else they should ask.
y-m-79-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write what two parts make 590 in calculation above.
y-m-79-03.s.s3.hint.1: Find which two values must change for size of those parts to change.
y-m-79-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Defective products are ... of total
y-m-79-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You distinguish what 95% ratio refers to (share defects caught, or share judgments correct)?
y-m-79-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You use numbers explain why low defect rate means many normal products wrongly caught?
y-m-79-03.s.s3.model.0: Only 1% products defective, so normal items far more numerous. Even if just 5% of normal items wrongly flagged, that is 495, more than 95 real defects. So among defect flags, real defects only about 16%. Ask both defect prevalence and rate normal items wrongly flagged.
y-m-79-03.s.s3.model.1: Need know whether 95% means defect-detection rate or correct-judgment rate, plus defective share of all items. If normal-item false-positive rate high, many flagged may be normal.

y-m-79-01.title: What a Five-Number Summary Can Tell You
y-m-79-01.goal: From five-number summary (minimum, quartiles, median, maximum), separate certain from uncertain claims and create different data sets with same summary to show its limits.
y-m-79-01.material:
Teacher gives performance-assessment scores (0 to 50 points, all whole numbers) for 7 students in one class as five-number summary.

Minimum 10 points, first quartile 15, median 20, third quartile 30, maximum 50.

Convention: sorted scores x1...x7: minimum=x1, Q1=x2, median=x4, Q3=x6, maximum=x7. Students may share a score. 0 50 7 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 1 2 4 6 7
y-m-79-01.thinking.1: Making different data sets with same summary (counterexamples)
y-m-79-01.prereq.0: Task is H3 hard level, assumed high-school elective Practical Statistics; not a Ministry grade assignment. Prerequisites: sort data, find median/quartiles, understand mean. For 7 data points quartiles are 2nd, 4th, 6th values (textbooks may differ).
y-m-79-01.s.s1.prompt: Knowing only summary, select all definitely true statements.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.hint.0: Draw 7 boxes x1–x7 and fill scores summary gives.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.hint.1: Identify which box each choice refers to; see if value fixed or blank.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.r.a: Mean isn't in summary. Median and mean differ; treating middle value as mean assumes all scores near 20.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.r.b: By convention median is fourth value; summary directly gives it. 4
y-m-79-01.s.s1.o.c: Exactly two students scored 30 or more.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.r.c: Even if x6=30, x5 could also be 30; can't say exactly two. 30 30 5 30
y-m-79-01.s.s1.o.d: At least 4 students scored 20 or more.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.r.d: Since x4=20, x5,x6,x7 can't be below it. Order gives at least four. 20 4
y-m-79-01.s.s1.r.e: x3 or x5 could also be 20. Summary value may occur more than once.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.explain: There are 7 students; fourth is median 20, and students 4–7 have 20 or more, so at least 4 is certain. But x3 only known between 15 and 20, x5 between 20 and 30; exact values unknown. Mean, exact count at 30+, and exact count at 20 aren't determined by summary alone. 7 4 20 4 7 20 4 15 20 20 30 30 20
y-m-79-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 score sets with same summary (x1=10,x2=15,x4=20,x6=30,x7=50) but different means. Enter 7 scores sorted.
y-m-79-01.s.s2.hint.0: Fill x1,x2,x4,x6,x7 from summary first; identify two blank boxes.
y-m-79-01.s.s2.hint.1: Find possible ranges for blanks by comparing neighboring scores.
y-m-79-01.s.s2.hint.2: Add each data set and check means differ.
y-m-79-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Not sorted; an earlier value can't exceed a later one.
y-m-79-01.s.s3.prompt: If two classes have same box plot but different means, what tell someone comparing means from plots alone? You may use your data.
y-m-79-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write mean of both data sets you made.
y-m-79-01.s.s3.hint.1: Separately write one thing box plot shows and one it doesn't.
y-m-79-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Means are about 22.9 and 25 points, so ...
y-m-79-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you cite mean (or total) as evidence?
y-m-79-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you distinguish 'same box plot' from 'same mean'?
y-m-79-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say what box plot can show (e.g., median, spread)?
y-m-79-01.s.s3.model.0: Two sets share min, quartiles, median and max, but means differ (about 22.9 and 25). Same box plot doesn't mean same mean; don't compare means using box plot alone. Median and spread can be compared.
y-m-79-01.s.s3.model.1: Even if only x3,x5 change, mean changes while five-number summary remains. Summary doesn't determine mean; need original scores if mean matters.
y-m-79-01.s.s3.model.2: Two data sets can share summary but differ in x3,x5 and mean. Comparing means from box plots alone can be wrong.

y-m-79-06.topic: Expected value and design fair game
y-m-79-06.title: Set festival draw prize amounts
y-m-79-06.goal: Use expected value to design several entry fee/prize setups and explain one draw versus long-run average.
y-m-79-06.material:
At school festival our class runs prize draw. Box has 100 slips; participant pays entry fee f원 and draws one (calculations use average per slip).
- 1 first-prize slip: gift card P원
- 9 second-prize slips: gift card 2000원
- Other 90 slips: blank
Our class pays face value of cards; no other costs. Student says, "I paid 1000원, won first prize gift card, so draw favors participants."
y-m-79-06.thinking.0: Spot error in judging from one result
y-m-79-06.thinking.2: Explain difference between average and variation
y-m-79-06.prereq.0: Task H3 assumes high-school Practical Statistics, not ministry grade assignment. Prereq expected value meaning/calculation (prize×probability sum). Here read as average payout per slip. Law of large numbers only intuitive.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.hint.0: First find total gift-card amount across all 100 slips.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare average per slip (total ÷100) with entry fee.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.o.a: One result can't tell. Need average payout across all slips.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.r.a: Judge by average over many attempts, not one result.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.o.b: Only 1 first prize, probability 1%, so draw surely bad for participants.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.r.b: You look only first-prize probability. Include 9 second prizes in average.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.o.c: One attempt gives surest evidence, so claim correct.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.r.c: One person's result may be chance. Repeated plays approach average.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.o.d: Expected value always equals one draw payout, so calculation exact for single attempt.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.r.d: Expected value means long-run average; need not match one outcome.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.explain: Chance affects single result. Whether game favorable depends on comparing entry fee with average across 100 slips (expected value).
y-m-79-06.s.s2.prompt: Choose first-prize amount P (원) and fee f (원) so class meets two conditions. Make 3 designs. (1) Average payout per slip ≤f, so class doesn't lose on average. (2) Participant average loss per slip f−payout ≤300원. P in 1000원 units from 5000 to 30000; f in 100원 units 100 to 1000.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.hint.0: Choose P, sum first and nine second prizes, divide by 100. nine second prizes. 9 cards.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.hint.1: Using average payout as base, find lower/upper fee range, then choose a 100원-unit value.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.ok.c1: First prize stays in required range/unit.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.fail.c3: Average payout per slip exceeds entry fee, so class loses on average. Compare f with total first and second prizes divided by 100.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.ok.c4: Participant average loss is at most 300원.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.explain: Average payout per slip = (P+9×2000)÷100 = P÷100+180원. Example P=10000 gives 280원, so f range 280–580원; 300,400,500원 in 100원 steps work. If P=20000, average 380원, so f range 400–680원. 300, 400, 500, 400, 680.
y-m-79-06.s.s3.prompt: Teacher asks, "We set price using expected value, but if only 10 people draw lots, will class total gain/loss match plan? What about 100 people? Compare and answer." 10 100
y-m-79-06.s.s3.hint.0: For 10 people, suppose first prize either doesn't appear or appears once; say how much total payout differs. 10
y-m-79-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare in one sentence how average per ticket changes as participants increase.
y-m-79-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: More tickets sold, closer to average ...
y-m-79-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you describe difference when few and many participate?
y-m-79-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain in your own words expected value is average, not each outcome?
y-m-79-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you imagine a concrete way class could lose with 10 people? 10
y-m-79-06.s.s3.model.0: As more tickets sell, average gain/loss per ticket tends toward expected value, so plan becomes more accurate. With 10, first prize may or may not happen by chance, so total can differ greatly. 10
y-m-79-06.s.s3.model.1: Expected value is average over many trials. Even with 100, exactly one first prize isn't guaranteed, but gap from average tends smaller. With only 10, chance matters greatly; class may lose. 100 10

y-m-79-02.title: Which of two practice methods works better?
y-m-79-02.goal: Show with data that overall proportion and within-group proportions can point opposite ways; judge reliable comparison and needed information.
y-m-79-02.material: 700 running-club members tried one of two methods for a month, then were asked if they met personal target time. Members chose method and course (easy or hard) themselves. 350 chose A, 350 chose B. Achievement rate = achievers ÷ group size.
y-m-79-02.thinking.0: Revising or keeping judgment as data grows
y-m-79-02.prereq.0: Task H3 hard level for Practical Statistics elective, not grade assignment. Prerequisites: calculate/compare proportions and compare groups with same total; no probability formulas needed.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.prompt: One piece of data appears each step. Choose judgment based on current info; you needn't change earlier view.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each method/course cell, divide achievers by cell total, table results, compare methods within same course.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.hint.1: Show counts in easy and hard courses for both methods; see which group's overall rate resembles more.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.info: Overall: A 273 of 350 met target; B 289 of 350.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: From data so far, which method seems more effective?
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.after: Overall rate A about 78.0%, B about 82.6%. Reasonable to say B higher; also reasonable to hold off because members chose themselves.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: A more effective. Group sizes same, so A members did better.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: B had more achievers. Recheck counts to see which higher.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: B seems more effective: of same 350, more achieved.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You read numbers correctly. Next step can check if this is method effect.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I won't decide yet. Members self-selected, so need know more about who chose each.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You first considered that chooser characteristics may mix into result.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Methods same. Achiever counts similar, 273 and 289.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Difference of 16 people too soon to call same. Convert to rates and compare.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now which method seems more effective?
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.after: A rate higher in both courses. Overall B higher, suggesting course mix may differ greatly by method.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Calculation must be wrong. If A higher in both, B can't be higher overall.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Recalculate totals/rates: all correct. This can happen when group sizes differ.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: I keep first judgment B. Overall higher and group sizes equal, so fairest comparison.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: We haven't checked course mix across methods. Equal total group size doesn't mean same mix.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: I lean toward A. Within each course A is higher.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You think to compare under same conditions. Next step checks why overall result opposite.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Don't decide. A higher in each course, but first check course composition for each method.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This judgment wants to check mix when results conflict. Next info gives exactly that.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.info: Course choices: among A's 350, 263 (75.1%) chose hard; among B's 350, 270 (77.1%) chose easy. Easy course has higher achievement for both methods.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which comparison more trustworthy for judging method effect?
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.after: Comparing within course reduces difficulty influence, but members still self-selected method. If more capable people chose one method, ability mixes with method effect. So it's fitting to say within-course comparison more trustworthy, but still uncertain.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Overall comparison more trustworthy. Both groups 350, so fair.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Equal group sizes don't mean difficulty mix equal. A has more hard-course members.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Look only at hard course. Result with more people (263 vs 80) more reliable.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Hard-course B has only 80; using one course throws out other-course info.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Within-course comparison better because difficulty affects achievement.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You filter out difficulty, but reason for course choice (e.g. ability) remains.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Still hard to be sure. Within-course comparison better, but self-selection may leave ability differences.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You considered observational-data limits; this explains need for random assignment.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.reflect: How did judgment differ from step 1 to step 3? Overall rate first seemed convincing; what made comparison less reliable? If kept judgment, what extra evidence did you add?
y-m-79-02.s.s2.prompt: Club wants to check method effect more reliably. Which approach best?
y-m-79-02.s.s2.hint.0: Compare who decides which person uses each method and course.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.hint.1: For each method, write one reason mix may be uneven; mark approach that removes it.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.o.a: Double members and survey the same way (self-selection).
y-m-79-02.s.s2.r.a: More people won't remove same self-selection imbalance. More data and fair comparison are different.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.o.b: Recommend B to everyone because overall rate higher; don't investigate further.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.r.b: Overall rate from uneven mix ignores A's higher rate within each course.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.o.c: Assign members randomly to methods and have them practice on same course.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.r.c: Random choice reduces imbalance in ability and course.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.o.d: Collect/read reviews from A users in hard course.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.r.d: Reviews give reasons, but reviewers are also self-selected, weak for comparison.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.explain: Randomly assign similar groups at start and have same conditions; then result difference more plausibly comes from method. Increasing headcount alone doesn't remove imbalance.
y-m-79-02.s.s3.prompt: Member says, 'B overall achievement higher, so B better, right?' Answer using one or two numbers.
y-m-79-02.s.s3.hint.0: Find which group's total the cited number represents.
y-m-79-02.s.s3.hint.1: Choose one number from same-course groups and use it in answer.
y-m-79-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: B higher overall, but course mix ...
y-m-79-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is it clear which group's achievement rate your number refers to?
y-m-79-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain opposite overall result using course mix?
y-m-79-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you mention limits of self-selection, even briefly?
y-m-79-02.s.s3.model.0: B looks higher overall, but most B members (270) chose easy course, while most A (263) chose hard. Within easy, A 93%, B 87%; within hard A 73%, B 69%. So A higher within each; overall alone doesn't prove B better.
y-m-79-02.s.s3.model.1: Difficulty affects success, and course mixes differ, so overall rates aren't fair comparison. By course A higher both times. But they chose methods themselves; random assignment and another check would be more certain.
y-m-79-02.s.s3.model.2: Easy course A 93%, B 87%; hard A 73%, B 69%, so A higher. B overall higher because more B members were on easy course.

y-m-79-05.title: Are all top-ranked schools small schools?
y-m-79-05.goal: Explain using student count and average fluctuation why small schools appear at both ranking ends; suggest redesign to prevent misreading.
y-m-79-05.material:
Article introduces schools' academic-test averages (out of 100) in region: "Top 3 average-score schools all small, with 15 or fewer test takers. Small schools have higher achievement."
Top 3: School 가 9 students, 91.2; School 나 15, 89.0; School 다 12, 87.5.
y-m-79-05.prereq.0: Task H3 assumes high-school elective Practical Statistics, not ministry grade assignment. Prereqs: mean meaning and SD intuition ('how scores spread from mean'). Standard-error formula (σ÷√n) useful beforehand but not required.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.prompt: Using only these 3 schools, best judgment on claim 'small schools higher achievement'?
y-m-79-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write which school range article selected.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write in one line what other school data needed to test same claim.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.o.a: We can say small schools advantaged; all top 3 small.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.r.a: This only looks at high end. Without checking whether small schools also low, you accept selectively presented result.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.o.b: We can say small schools disadvantaged because average unstable when student count low.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.r.b: Average instability matters, but this data alone can't show disadvantage direction.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.o.c: Too early to judge. We don't know spread of averages among all small schools.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.r.c: This checks whether only top-three data support claim. Top 3.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.r.d: Even objective numbers, claim depend on which schools chosen.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.explain: Article only show highest averages. Whether small schools overall high or scattered high and low can be known only with lower-end and large-school data.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.prompt: Education office released other 6 schools. Others: Ra School 11 students avg 64.3; Ma 14 avg 66.0; Ba 120 avg 78.4; Sa 150 avg 77.9; A 210 avg 78.8; Ja 240 avg 77.5. Now best interpretation of article's claim and data?
y-m-79-05.s.s2.hint.0: Sort all 9 schools by average, mark small and large differently.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.hint.1: Split into 5 small and 4 large schools; give highest and lowest average for each.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.o.a: Keep article claim. Top 3 all small, so effect clear.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.r.a: Bottom 2 also small. With added data, 'effect is clear' has weak support.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.o.b: Small schools actually disadvantaged; bottom 2 both small.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.r.b: Now you only looked at bottom and reversed conclusion. Also note top 3 are small.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.o.c: Data contradict, so no conclusion either way; discard it.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.r.c: This isn't contradiction but a pattern. Small-school averages on both high/low ends while large schools cluster is meaningful.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.o.d: Fewer students make school average swing up/down more easily. That's why small schools cluster at both extremes.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.r.d: You consider extremes both ways. This fits explanation that fewer students means chance swings average more.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.explain: Overall, 5 small schools at extremes: 91.2,89.0,87.5,66.0,64.3; 4 large schools cluster 77.5–78.8. If individual SD about 12, average of 9 students has standard error about 4.0; average for 210 or 240 students about 0.8. Fewer students means more average movement.
y-m-79-05.s.s3.prompt: Education office wants change ranking table to avoid misunderstanding. Suggest at least one edit and explain why it helps.
y-m-79-05.s.s3.hint.0: Find info missing from ranking table that helps judge trustworthiness of averages.
y-m-79-05.s.s3.hint.1: Write how reading small-school ranks changes if you add that info.
y-m-79-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Include student count in ranking, and ...
y-m-79-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is additional info in proposal clear?
y-m-79-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does proposal relate to small schools crowding both ranking extremes?
y-m-79-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You think about downside too (e.g. table gets complicated)?
y-m-79-05.s.s3.model.0: Show student count and rank schools in similar-size groups. Few students mean average moves with just a few scores, so chance can put school high or low.
y-m-79-05.s.s3.model.1: Use several-year average rather than one year, and show margin of error. Small schools' scores jump year to year, so one-year result hard to trust.
y-m-79-05.s.s3.model.2: Show student count and margin of error for low-count schools. Few students make average change a lot with a few scores.

y-m-79-07.title: Plant height report: predicting 20 weeks later 20
y-m-79-07.topic: Interpreting regression line and predicting beyond data range
y-m-79-07.goal: Distinguish line fitting observed range from trusting extrapolation; rewrite prediction with conditions.
y-m-79-07.material: Student measures potted plant weekly. Heights (cm), weeks 1–6: 5.1,8.4,11.3,14.8,18.0,21.1 (points nearly straight line). Student finds least-squares line. Results: slope about 3.2, intercept 1.9, correlation 0.9998. x means number of weeks. 1 6 5.1 8.4 11.3 14.8 18.0 21.1 3.2 1.9 0.9998
y-m-79-07.thinking.1: Judging information needed to trust prediction
y-m-79-07.prereq.0: Task H3 hard level for Practical Statistics elective, not Ministry grade. Prerequisites: scatterplot/correlation show linear relation strength and interpreting slope. Line equation supplied; no need calculate it.
y-m-79-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose report line with wrong interpretation.
y-m-79-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, say whether week number is inside/outside measured range (week 1–6). 1 6
y-m-79-07.s.s1.hint.1: For outside prediction, consider which weeks high correlation refers to.
y-m-79-07.s.s1.line.0: Line for weeks 1–6: height ≈ 3.2×weeks +1.9 cm; correlation about 0.9998. 1 6 3.2 1.9 0.9998
y-m-79-07.s.s1.line.1: Correlation near 1, so line explains data well within measured weeks 1–6. 1 1 6
y-m-79-07.s.s1.line.3: Week 20 height is 3.2×20+1.9=65.9 cm; since correlation high, week 20 will also be about 66 cm. 20 3.2 20 1.9 65.9 66 20
y-m-79-07.s.s1.line.4: Slope 3.2 means during measured period height grew about 3.2 cm per week on average. 3.2 3.2
y-m-79-07.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is wrong. Calculation 3.2×20+1.9=65.9 is right, but high correlation means good fit only in measured weeks 1–6. It doesn't guarantee same growth at unmeasured week 20. Lines 1–3 and 5 are right. 4 3.2 20 1.9 65.9 1 6 20 1 3 5
y-m-79-07.s.s2.prompt: What information needed to judge whether week-20 prediction trustworthy? Select all needed. 20
y-m-79-07.s.s2.hint.0: Separate info that tells actual week-20 height from info only making line for weeks 1–6 more precise. 20 1 6
y-m-79-07.s.s2.hint.1: For each option, ask whether it would let you check prediction right/wrong. 20
y-m-79-07.s.s2.o.a: Correlation recalculated with more decimal places
y-m-79-07.s.s2.r.a: This gives more precision for fit within weeks 1–6, not growth at week 20. 1 6 20
y-m-79-07.s.s2.o.b: Info about whether growth speed continues after week 6 (maximum height, environment) 6
y-m-79-07.s.s2.r.b: You choose info directly about how growth outside range may change.
y-m-79-07.s.s2.o.c: Measure weeks 1–6 again same way and refit line 1 6
y-m-79-07.s.s2.r.c: More data within same range makes line more precise, but outside growth still unknown.
y-m-79-07.s.s2.o.d: Actual height measurements of same plant type after week 10 10
y-m-79-07.s.s2.r.d: This lets you check actual values beyond range directly against prediction.
y-m-79-07.s.s2.explain: Outside-range prediction assumes same relationship continues there. Only growth characteristics or actual measurements after week 10 can test assumption. More precise weeks 1–6 data don't confirm it. 10 1 6
y-m-79-07.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite report's week-20 prediction (line 4) with conditions. Keep 66 cm, but show how to interpret it. 4 20 66
y-m-79-07.s.s3.hint.0: Include measured week range as written.
y-m-79-07.s.s3.hint.1: Use 'if...' to state assumption required for 66 cm. 66
y-m-79-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does sentence make reader treat 66 cm as conditional value, not certain fact? 66
y-m-79-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you distinguish prediction inside range (e.g. week 3.5) from outside? 3.5
y-m-79-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you mention one reason line may not fit (growth slowing/stopping)?
y-m-79-07.s.s3.model.0: Line fits weeks 1–6, but 20 is outside measurements; 66 cm only if plant keeps growing at same rate. In reality growth may slow or stop. 1 6 20 66
y-m-79-07.s.s3.model.1: 66 cm at week 20 assumes growth after week 6 stays same speed. We only measured through week 6, so can't know; measure near week 20 to check. 20 66 6 6 20
